parties:
State ------ Appellant
Vs.
Md. Mominullah (Mohan) & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: These appeals arose by way of leave granted in Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 256-260 of 1998 filed against the judgment and order dated 24-6-1998 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case Nos. 2693, 2993, 2994 of 1997 and Criminal Miscellaneous Case Nos. 771 and 981 of 1998 quashing the proceedings in GR Case No. 247 of 1997 arising out of Satkhira PS Case No.18 dated 19-6-1996 pending in the Court of Sessions Judge, Satkhira giving rise to Sessions Case No. 57 of 1997 discharging the accused-respondents from the case and from their respective bail bonds. 

 2. One Md Nasiruddin Sardar lodged first information report with Satkhira Police Station on 19-6-1996 at 11-15 PM alleging that at about 10-40 PM he got an information that his brother SM. Alauddin, a Freedom Fighter and the editor of Pa tradoot Patrika, sustained gunshot injury. He rushed to Satkhira Sadar Hospital and found his brother Alauddin dead. On hearing gun shot in the office of the said Patrika the police personnel of Satkhira Police Station and an editor of another newspaper rushed to the place of occurrence and found Alauddin in his chair in dying condition with head injury. Immediately they brought him to the hospital where the doctor declared him dead. The informant alleged in the first information report (FIR) that some unknown miscreants shot at his brother and killed him and he demanded investigation into the case. 

 3. That the instant criminal case was started on the basis of the said first information report. One co-accused made a confessional statement. Several witnesses were examined under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and charge-sheet was admitted under sections 302/34 of the Penal Code against the respondents and others. Five accused persons filed separate applications in the High Court Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceedings and Rules were obtained. 

 4. That the High Court Division quashed the proceeding on the ground, inter alia, that no name of any accused has been mentioned in the first information report, that the confessional statement of one of the accused namely, Kazi Saiful Islam, dated 29-6-96 is exculpatory and cannot be accepted as evidence and cannot be relied upon. The name of accused respondent Md Mominullah (Mohon) was mentioned in the confessional statement not in connection with the occurrence itself but in connection with alleged collection of arms on a subsequent date. The confessional statement was not supported by any other independent materials. The witnesses were examined on two dates by the police under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The names of the respondents do not feature in the first examination under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Even if their names feature in the second examination under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the statements do not disclose any offence with regard to the respondents in the instant case. There is total lack of materials against the respondents to implicate them in the murder case. The charge-sheet submitted against them is illegal and the respondents cannot be harassed in such a murder case. It will be an abuse of the process of the Court and, in order to secure the ends of justice, the proceeding against them should be quashed. 

 5. The High Court Division discussed the GD Entry the first information report and the statements made under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and found that the involvement of the respondents in the crime is not disclosed in those materials. The name of the respondent Md Abul Kalam alias Kalam was not mentioned in the first information report or in the confessional statement or in the statements recorded under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Respondent MA Rouf alias Md Abdur Rouf Sardar stands on the same footing with respondent Md Abul Kalam alias Kalam. In the confessional statement the former Chairman respondent Abdur Rouf Sardar of Nagurghata Union Parishad was stated to have been serving a sentence in jail in connection with a criminal case at the relevant time. Respondents AI Haj Md Abdus Sabur and Md Khalilullah alias Jharu are stated to have offered a bribe for murdering Alauddlin which was a hearsay statement from one Kislu to the confessing accused. Such statements will not bind in any manner the said respondents in the instant case. 

 7. Mr Faisal H Khan, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing with Mr Abdur Razzaque Khan, the learned Additional Attorney-General for the appellant, submitted that the High Court Division indulged in an unacceptable exercise in treating the GD Entry the first information report, the statement under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the alibi of some accused respondents, as if those are admissible evidence in a trial and like a trial Court the High Court Division has given a judgment of acquittal on the basis of those materials without giving a thought that the only jurisdiction which the High Court Division has under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is whether prima facie, there are materials admissible in evidence or relevant or can be relied upon or are sufficient or not. The learned Assistant Attorney-General further submitted that an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is premature at the initial stage under the facts and circumstances of the case unless the accused-respondent had gone through the stage under section 265C of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as such, the High Court Division erred in law in quashing the proceeding. 

 8. Mr TH Khan with Mr Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Counsels appearing for the respondents, submitted that in the instant case, there is no materials on record to connect the respondents directly with the commission of the alleged offence and, as such, the High Court Division in exercise of its inherent power under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure has rightly quashed the proceeding so far it relates to the accused-respondents. The learned Counsel further submitted that in exercise of its inherent power, the High Court Division has rightly found that the confessional statement is exculpatory and narrative or informative in nature, as because on being accompanied by the accused namely, Saiful Islam alias Kislu, the confessing accused did not play any active role in the commission of the alleged offence, rather on every occasion he left the place of occurrence by running and, on the other hand, with regard to the motive of killing the victim, the confessing accused Kazi Saiful Islam narrated a story what he was told by the accused Saiful Islam alias Kislu and that the witnesses having been examined twice under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure there was material alteration relating and embellishment in between the two statements of the concerned witnesses examining within a span of almost one month and accordingly, the High Court Division on application of judicial mind considering the statement including the confessional statement of accused Saiful Islam which is exculpatory in nature, has rightly quashed the proceeding against the accused-respondent to secure ends of justice and to prevent abuse of the process of the Court. 

 11. The aforesaid statements prima facie implicated the accused respondents in the case and the police upon investigation has submitted charge-sheet against the accused including the accused respondents. After issuance of these Rules by the High Court Division out of which the present appeal arose, the learned Sessions Judge upon examination of the record and the materials along with it and hearing the parties framed charges against the accused including the accused-respondents. 

 12. The principle of quashing proceeding has been formulated in the celebrated decision in the case of Abdul Quader vs State reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38 wherein it was held that: 

 "Ordinarily, criminal proceedings instituted against an accused person must be tried under the provisions of the Code and the said proceedings should not be generally interfered with at an interlocutory stage in exercise of the inherent jurisdiction provided under section 561-A of the Code. But a pertinent question may be posed as to when and under what circumstances the said jurisdiction can and should be exercised by the High Court. The consensus of judicial opinion is that it is not possible, desirable or expedient to lay down any inflexible rule which should govern the exercise of this inherent jurisdiction. The exercise of this jurisdiction will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts no case can stand against the accused and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the Court. Besides, some categories of cases may also be indicated where the inherent jurisdiction can and should be exercised for quashing the proceeding. There may be cases where it may be possible for the High Court to take the view that the institution or continuance of criminal proceedings against an accused person may amount to the abuse of the process of the Court or that the quashing of the impugned proceedings would secure the ends of justice. If the criminal proceedings in question is in respect of an offence alleged to have been committed by an accused person and it manifestly appears that there is a legal bar against the institution or continuance of the said proceedings the High Court would be justified in quashing the proceedings on that ground. Cases may also arise where the allegations in the first information report or the complaint even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence alleged. In such cases no question of appreciating evidence arises, it is a matter merely of looking at the complaint or the first information report to decide whether the offence alleged is disclosed or not. In such cases it would be legitimate for the High Court to hold that it would be manifestly unjust to allow process of the criminal Court to be issued against the accused person. A third category of cases in which the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court can be invoked may also arise. In cases falling under this category the allegations made against the accused person do constitute an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. In dealing with this class of cases it is important to bear in mind the distinction between a case where there is no legal evidence or where there is evidence which is manifestly and clearly inconsistent with the accusation made and cases where there is legal evidence which on its appreciation may not support the accusation in question. In exercising the jurisdiction under section 561A, the High Court would not embark upon an enquiry as to whether the evidence in question is reliable or not. That is the function of the trial Magistrate and ordinarily, it would not be open to any party to invoke the High Court's inherent jurisdiction and contend that on a reasonable appreciation of the evidence the accusation made against the accused would not be sustained. Broadly speaking, that is the nature and scope of the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court under section 561-A in the matter of quashing criminal proceedings. Reference on this point may be made to some of the decisions, namely, Ghulam Muhammad vs Muzammel Khan reported in PLD 1967 (SC) 317, Gianchand vs State reported in 1968 Pakistan Criminal Law Journal (SC) 764, RP Kapur vs State of Punjab reported in AIR 1960 (SC) 866, MS Khawaja vs State reported in 17 DLR (SC) 153. This being the legal position the question which arises for our decision is whether the present case falls under any of the categories mentioned above. In our view, there appears to be no legal bar to the institution of the present proceedings or their continuance. It has, however, been contended that the allegations made in the first information report do not constitute the offence alleged against the appellants especially in view of the agreement between the Firm and the Coal Controller. This contention has no force in view of the fact that the police of the Anti-Corruption Branch considered the alleged offence to be a cognisable one and on completion of investigation submitted charge-sheet. The learned Magistrate having been satisfied about the prima facie case after submission of the charge-sheet by the police has issued warrant of arrest. In such circumstances it is difficult to say that there were no materials justifying the submission of charge-sheet. The present case, in our view, should be proceeded with to ensure that the course of even handed justice is not interrupted. For reasons considered above we are of the view that the High Court has rightly refused to quash the proceeding in exercise of powers under section 561A. 

 These appeals are accordingly dismissed. The records be sent down immediately for expeditious disposal of the case." 

 13. Though it is not possible to suggest any yardstick or situation as to when and how a proceeding should be quashed at an interlocutory stage but the exercise of jurisdiction will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Though it is not desirable to lay down any inflexible rule governing the fields of quashing a proceeding but in aforesaid decision certain circumstances have been detailed for the purpose namely, when the first information report or the complaint even if taken at its face value and accepted in its entirety, do not constitute an offence, where facts are so preposterous that even on admitted facts no case stands against the accused or on the facts alleged it manifestly appears that there is a legal bar against the institution or prolongation of the proceeding. 

 14. In the instant case, the first information report dated 19-6-1996 was lodged at 12-45 PM though disclosed an, offence committed by some unknown miscreant but has not named anybody implicated with the offence. In the course of investigation both by the Police and the CLD certain witnesses/accused were examined under sections 161 and 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and upon completion of the investigation the Police submitted charge-sheet No.136 dated 6-5-1997 against respondents and others as it transpires and a prima facie case against the accused under sections 302/120B/109/34 of the Penal Code. 

 15. Mr TH Khan, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondents, has referred to a decision in the case of Mofazzal Hossain Mollah and others vs State reported in 45 DLR (AD) 175 in support of his submissions that the confessional statement of the accused Saiful Islam was made after being taken on remand and inhuman torture perpetuated on him and produced him before the Magistrate to make a tutored statement which he at the earliest opportunity retracted and the same could not be the basis for any prosecution even if the same may be incriminating in nature. 

 "It is further seen that two judgments, one in appeal and one by the Court of first instance, were passed in this case and all against the petitioners and this is also against him. How many times the petitioners will challenge a judgment and lastly, in a quashing petition, which is not at all maintainable." 

 The learned Judges proceeded on the assumption that section 561A, CrPC is meant only for quashing a criminal proceeding before the trial has started and that when the trial, as in this case, has been concluded, followed by an appeal and a revision, both being unsuccessful, how the convicted accused could come under this section for quashing the proceeding. Section 561A has only reiterated the Court's inherent power to give effect to any order under the Code of Criminal Procedure "to prevent the abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the enci8 of justice". In this case, the appellants invoked the inherent power of the Court to secure ends of justice by getting the order of their conviction quashed or set aside on the ground that the conviction was based on no evidence. The learned Judges failed to exercise their power under this section to look into the matter and see whether the conviction was valid and legal or whether it was invalid on the very face of it for want of any legal evidence to support it. The fact that the accused were tried and found guilty and then unsuccessfully filed an appeal and a revisional application cannot be a ground, in the facts of the present case, for refusing to exercise the Court's power under section 561A, CrPC." 

 18. The learned Counsel has also referred to an unreported decision in the case of Tariqul Islam vs State in Criminal Appeal Nos. 37-38 of 2001 in which My Lord the Chief Justice and myself are parties, suggesting the touchstone required for quashing a proceeding terming the confessional statement of accused Kazi Saiful Islam as one exculpatory in nature and the same was obtained after he was taken to police custody on remand and for which the same could not be regarded as voluntary as the same was obtained by torture and duress and more-so, the same was retracted soon thereafter. But the fact of the said case is fundamentally different from the instant case because of the confessing accused none of them has implicated accused appellant therein. On the contrary, out of the 5 accused persons making confessional statements, 3 out of them did not state anything about the accused but the statement of the two accused though alleged to be at the residence of the accused at the same time but made contradictory statements opposing each other regarding the events at the residence of the appellant inasmuch as they did not say anything to implicate the accused appellant in any way. 

 19. The learned Counsel for the accused further submitted that the confessional statement, even admitting the same to be inculpatory in nature but the alleged implication of the accused was by way of narration of the facts which are informative in nature and could not be the basis for taking cognisance against them with the alleged offence, and has referred to a decision in the case of Zabaida Rashid vs Bangladesh reported in 2 BLC 356. In the said decision the statement of the witnesses did not have the effect of implicating the accused with the offence. 

 20. In the instant case, as we have already observed, that the statements under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are all statements of the witnesses which were made in the course of investigation and those are no evidence in the case. So far the statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is concerned, confession of a co-accused though not a substantive evidence against other accused, the Court may take such confession into consideration and use the same to lend assurance to other evidence for the purpose of conviction. It is also now a well-founded proposition of law that the statement of an accused person which is not a confession but contains an admission of certain relevant facts is admissible under sections 18-21 of the Evidence Act, provided it is voluntary, even though retracted, if found to be true by the trial Court which is required to be corroborated by evidence of other witnesses in order to be the basis for conviction of the co-accused respondents and, as regards statement under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the same is a statement and is not an evidence in the case and, as such, not at all admissible in law unless the witnesses are confronted with the said statement while deposing on dock having deposed contrary to the said statement, the same could not be of any avail to the prosecution but the statement could be utilised under section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to contradict the witness in the manner provided under section 145 of the Evidence Act. Thus the statement under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is restricted to an investigation by the police for the purpose of police report. 

 21. The exercise of inherent power under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure should be limited to the objects detailed in the section itself but the same does not appear to be exhaustive but remained to be undefined and indefinite and must be exercised with utmost caution lest under the garb of exercise of inherent jurisdiction, a great injustice is not perpetrated at the initial stage of the case when, as a matter of fact, there is no evidence before the Court in the case except certain allegation. 

 22. The Court obviously could not shut its eyes to the apparent infirmities in the case and, as such, in order to prevent abuse of the process of the Court or otherwise to secure ends of justice such exercise of jurisdiction becomes imperative in order to avoid any unnecessary harassment to the accused under the garb of dispensation of justice. But in doing so the Court could not enter into merit as to the allegation at the initial stage soon after the investigation unless the illegality is apparent on the face of the allegation which does not constitute an offence or there is legal bar to 'proceed. 

 23. Admittedly, there are some statements or materials to implicate the accused in the case, on consideration of which a prima facie case being made out upon investigation, the police has submitted the charge-sheet against the accused including the respondent in the case. It is not that there is no statement or material to implicate the respondent prima facie in the case and, as such, we do not find any substance in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the respondents. There being prima facie statement implicating the accused with the offence along with other accused we find substance in the appeal. 

 24. It may be observed that our finding or observations above shall have no bearing and should not in any way influence the trial Court at the trial of the case. 

 Accordingly, these appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division discharging the accused-respondents in the case are hereby set aside and the accused-respondents are directed to appear before the trial Court to face the trial in accordance with law.
